segments.text: Imagine you're moving, and you've narrowed it down to two towns.
Maple, and Pine Hill.
You look up the numbers, and both towns report the same average household income.
Sixty thousand dollars a year.
Same average. So, same kind of town, right?
Let's actually meet the families.
Maple has nine households.
Their incomes, in thousands of dollars, are fifty, fifty-two, fifty-five, fifty-eight, sixty, sixty-two, sixty-five, sixty-eight, and seventy.
Everyone is fairly close to sixty.
Now Pine Hill. Also nine households.
Eight of them earn between thirty and forty-eight thousand.
And one family earns two hundred thirty thousand dollars a year.
Add it all up and divide, and yes, Pine Hill's average is also sixty.
But look where the families actually are.
Eight out of nine households earn less than the average.
The average isn't technically wrong. But it describes a family that doesn't live there.
Today, we'll meet the two most common kinds of average: the mean, and the median.
And learn how to tell which one is lying to you.
This isn't just a puzzle about two made-up towns.
Every week, you hear averages in the news.
Average salary. Average house price. Average wait time at the hospital.
Each of those is one number standing in for thousands of people.
If it's the wrong kind of average, it can push you into a bad decision.
Like moving to Pine Hill expecting to earn what your neighbours earn.
Or opening a fancy restaurant there, counting on sixty-thousand-dollar customers who mostly aren't there.
The good news: telling the two averages apart takes a few minutes, and no fancy math.
Let's start with the one you already know: the mean.
The mean is what most people call 'the average'.
To find it, add up all the values, then divide by how many there are.
Let's do it for Pine Hill.
Thirty, plus thirty-two, plus thirty-five, and so on, all the way up to two hundred thirty.
The total is five hundred forty.
There are nine households, so we divide by nine.
Five hundred forty divided by nine is sixty.
In math books, you'll see this written as a formula. Let's decode it, one symbol at a time.
The letter x stands for one value. Here, one household's income.
The small i underneath means 'which one'. x one is the first household, x two is the second, and so on.
This big zigzag letter is the Greek capital sigma. It just means: add them all up.
The letter n means how many values there are. For Pine Hill, n is nine.
And the x with a bar on top, called x bar, is the name for the mean.
So the whole formula says: add up every value, then divide by how many there are.
But what is the mean, really? Here are two ways to picture it.
Picture one: fair shares.
Here are Pine Hill's nine incomes, as bars.
Imagine all nine families pour their income into one shared pot.
Then the pot is shared out equally, so every family gets the same amount.
Every bar ends up at exactly sixty. That's the mean.
So the mean answers one question: if everything were shared out evenly, how much would each get?
Picture two: a balance beam.
Put each household on the line as an equal weight, sitting at its income.
Where should the support go, so the beam balances perfectly?
Try forty. The beam tips to the right, because that one family is so far out.
Try sixty, and it balances.
Here's why. Measure how far each family is from sixty.
The eight families on the left are thirty, twenty-eight, twenty-five, twenty-two, twenty, eighteen, fifteen, and twelve below.
Together, that's one hundred seventy below.
And the one family on the right is one hundred seventy above.
The distances below and above cancel out exactly. That's what the mean always does.
And notice: one family, far enough away, balances eight families all by itself.
That's the mean's big weakness. Every value pulls on it, and the farther away a value is, the harder it pulls.
Now, the second kind of average: the median.
The median is the middle value, once the values are in order.
Step one: sort. Line the incomes up from smallest to largest.
Thirty, thirty-two, thirty-five, thirty-eight, forty, forty-two, forty-five, forty-eight, two hundred thirty.
Step two: find the middle. Cross one off each end, again and again, walking inward.
Thirty and two hundred thirty go. Then thirty-two and forty-eight. Then thirty-five and forty-five. Then thirty-eight and forty-two.
One value is left standing: forty.
The median income in Pine Hill is forty thousand dollars.
Four families earn less, and four earn more. That's the median's promise: it splits the group in half.
Compare that with the mean of sixty, where eight families were below and only one was above.
In Maple, the middle value is sixty, exactly the same as its mean.
You'll also hear the median called the fiftieth percentile, or p fifty, because it sits halfway through the sorted list.
But what if there's an even number of values? Then there's no single middle.
Say a new family moves to Pine Hill, earning fifty thousand.
Now there are ten households.
Cross off from both ends again, and this time two values are left in the middle: forty and forty-two.
The rule: take the halfway point between them. Add the two, and divide by two.
Forty plus forty-two is eighty-two. Half of that is forty-one.
So with ten families, the median is forty-one thousand.
And the mean? Five hundred ninety, divided by ten, which is fifty-nine.
For the rest of this video, let's go back to our original nine households.
So which average is more trustworthy? Let's stress test them.
Suppose Pine Hill's richest family has an amazing year.
Their income jumps from two hundred thirty thousand to two point three million. Ten times more.
Nobody else's income changes at all.
The new total is two thousand six hundred ten. Divided by nine, the mean becomes two hundred ninety thousand dollars.
According to the mean, the typical family is now almost five times richer. Yet not one of the other eight got a raise.
And the median? Sort, cross off, and the middle is still forty.
The median doesn't care how far away an extreme value is, only which side of the middle it's on.
Values that sit far away from the rest are called outliers.
The mean gets dragged toward outliers. The median hardly notices them. Statisticians call that being robust.
But being robust has a cost. Let's go back to two hundred thirty thousand, and this time, the poorest family's income falls from thirty thousand to ten.
Their life just got much harder. The mean dips, to about fifty-seven point eight.
The median stays at forty. It doesn't see the change at all.
The median ignores how far values are from the middle. The mean uses every bit of that. Each choice has a cost.
Now let's put everything back as it was, and step back to look at the shape of the data.
Maple's incomes are spread evenly around the middle. The left side is a mirror image of the right.
We call that symmetric. And for symmetric data, the mean and the median land in the same spot.
Pine Hill is lopsided: a crowd on the left, and a long, thin tail stretching off to the right.
That's called right-skewed. And in right-skewed data, the mean usually gets pulled toward the tail, past the median.
Flip it, with the tail on the left, and the mean usually lands below the median.
So here's a handy warning light: if the mean is much bigger than the median, a few large values are probably pulling it up.
One honest caveat: this is a rule of thumb, not a law. With oddly shaped data, it can fail. So always look at the actual values too.
So which average should you use? It depends on the question you're asking.
If your question is about totals, use the mean.
Say Pine Hill's town council wants to plan a budget from a two percent local income tax.
Total income is the mean times the number of households. Sixty times nine is five hundred forty thousand.
Two percent of that is ten thousand eight hundred dollars a year.
And the richest family alone pays more than forty percent of it. The council needs that outlier counted.
The median can't do this. Forty times nine is three hundred sixty, which misses a third of the real total.
But if your question is, what's life like for a typical family here, use the median.
If you move to Pine Hill, forty thousand is a far better guess for your neighbours' income than sixty.
And the mean and the median aren't the only options.
There's the mode, the value that appears most often. But no income in Pine Hill repeats, so here there isn't one.
There's also the trimmed mean: drop the most extreme values at each end, then take the mean of what's left.
Trim one from each end of Pine Hill, and the remaining seven add up to two hundred eighty. Divide by seven, and you get forty.
Here it happens to match the median exactly. In general, a trimmed mean sits somewhere between the two ideas: it uses most of the values, but one extreme one can't hijack it.
And when in doubt, report both the mean and the median. The gap between them tells you something too.
This choice shows up everywhere data is used. Let's visit four places.
First, money.
Incomes and house prices usually have a long right tail, just like Pine Hill: lots of ordinary values, and a few huge ones.
That's why the U.S. Census Bureau headlines median household income, not the mean.
And why housing reports usually quote the median sale price.
If a company advertises its average salary, ask whether the boss's pay is in there. One huge salary can lift the mean, just like Pine Hill's richest family.
Next, computer science. Think about how long a website takes to respond.
Most requests are quick, but now and then one gets stuck and takes ages.
It's the Pine Hill pattern again. A few slow requests drag the mean up, so it no longer describes a normal visit.
So engineers track the median, which they call p fifty, alongside the slow tail, such as p ninety-nine: the time that ninety-nine percent of requests beat or match.
In data science, one of the first jobs with new data is cleaning it.
Suppose the richest family's income was typed with one extra zero: two point three million instead of two hundred thirty thousand.
As we saw, that one typo drags the mean to two hundred ninety thousand. The median doesn't flinch.
So data scientists compare the mean and median as a quick check for typos and outliers. And when filling in missing values in skewed data, they often use the median.
Finally, machine learning. Here, the choice hides inside something called a loss function.
Imagine a model that must make one single guess for every Pine Hill family's income. What's the best guess?
It depends on how you score the mistakes.
Score one: add up how far off the guess is for each family. That's called absolute error.
Slide the guess along, and the total distance is smallest at forty. The median.
Score two: square each distance before adding, so big misses count extra. That's called squared error.
Now the best guess is sixty. The mean.
This works for any data, not just Pine Hill. Minimising squared error lands on the mean. Minimising absolute error lands on the median, or with an even count, anywhere between the two middle values.
So when someone trains a model with mean squared error or mean absolute error, they're choosing whether it aims for a mean or a median.
Squared error chases outliers. Absolute error shrugs them off. Same trade-off, new setting.
Before we wrap up, here are the three most common mistakes people make with averages.
Mistake one: taking the middle without sorting first.
Here are Pine Hill's incomes in the order the houses sit on the street: forty-two, two hundred thirty, thirty-five, forty-eight, thirty, forty-five, thirty-eight, thirty-two, and forty.
The middle of that list is thirty. That's not the median. It's just whoever lives in the middle house.
Always sort first. Sorted, the middle is forty.
Mistake two: assuming half the people are above the average.
That's true for the median, by design. It's not true for the mean.
In Pine Hill, only one family out of nine is above the mean. So if you're below average there, you're in very good company.
Mistake three: deciding the median is always better, and that outliers should just be deleted.
That rich family is real. Their income is real money, and the town's tax budget depends on it.
Remove a value only when you have evidence it's an error, like that extra zero. Otherwise keep it, and choose the average that fits your question.
And a bonus mistake: with an even count, picking one of the two middle numbers instead of the halfway point between them.
Let's turn all of that into a recipe you can use on any set of numbers.
Step one: sort the values, from smallest to largest.
Step two: find the mean. Add them all up, and divide by how many there are.
Step three: find the median, the middle value. With an even count, take the halfway point of the middle two.
Step four: compare them. If they're close, the data is probably fairly balanced. If the mean is much bigger, look for large values pulling it up.
Step five: match the average to your question. Totals and fair shares: the mean. A typical person or thing: the median. Not sure? Report both.
For Pine Hill, the mean is sixty, and the median is forty. Both are correct. They answer different questions.
An average only lies when you ask it the wrong question.
But here's a puzzle for next time.
Two towns can have the same mean and the same median, and still be completely different places to live.
The missing piece is spread: how far values typically sit from the middle.
Next time, we'll measure it with the standard deviation, and see why it squares the distances first.
See you in the lab.
